Mahipalpur to Gurugram Road, in front of Tata Telco, Vasant Kunj, New Delhi, regarding which one FIR No.254/18, U/s 279/337 IPC was registered at PS Vasant Kunj (South).

Onus to prove this issue was upon the claimant.
The claimant deposed as PW1.

She deposed that she along with her son Akhlesh Kumar, mother-in-law Smt. Parmeswari Devi, father-in-law Sh.

14.

15. PW1 was not cross-examined by the respondents regarding negligence.

Infact, during the course of final arguments, Ld. Counsel for respondent no. 3 conceded that the accident took place due to rash and negligent driving of respondent no. 1.

ISSUE NO. 2 - Whether the claimant is entitled for compensation?

If so, to what amount and from whom?
20.

As the issue No.1 has been decided in favour of the claimant, she has become entitled to be compensated for the injuries suffered by her in the accident, but the computation of compensation and liability to pay the same are required to be decided.
21. In terms of Section 168 of the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988, the compensation which is to be awarded by this Tribunal is required to be 'just'.
In injury cases, a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensation i.e. pecuniary as well as non- pecuniary damages.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar reported in (2011) 1 SCC 343, has laid down heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases as:-
Pecuniary damages (Special Damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising :
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General Damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).

(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
22.

Having considered the ratio of aforesaid judgment, the compensation payable to claimant is assessed hereinafter under the following heads as:-

5 (i) Medical or Treatment Expenses 23.

Claimant in her affidavit in evidence Ex. PW1/A, has tendered on record copy of medical treatment papers/OPD cards as Ex. PW1/1 (colly), as per which she was admitted in Safdarjung Hospital on 30.05.2018 and was discharged on the same day where she was diagnosed with post traumatic fracture L2 burst compression with intact neurology and without bladder bowel involvement.
Thereafter, she visited the OPD several times for follow up treatment.
24. Claimant has tendered on record her medical bills as Ex. PW1/2 (colly) which are in the sum of Rs.2,524.79.
During cross-examination, she volunteered that she has already submitted her medical bills along with the DAR and affidavit.
25. There are certain medical bills filed along with the DAR and affidavit which are in a sum of Rs.21,260/-.
The respondents have failed to lead any evidence to show that the said medical bills do not relate to the injuries suffered by the claimant in the aforesaid accident.
Thus, the testimony of PW-1 that she had spent the aforesaid amount towards medical expenses remained unrebutted and uncontroverted.
In the absence of any plausible evidence produced by respondents on record, there is no reason to disbelieve the testimony of PW-1 that she had spent the aforesaid amount towards medical expenses.
Hence, she is held entitled to Rs.21,260/- towards her medical expenses.
(ii) Loss of earnings 26.

The claimant in her affidavit Ex. PW1/A has deposed that she was doing private job of thread cutter with M/s Greenback International Pvt. Ltd., Okhla Industrial Area, New Delhi and was posted at Udyog Vihar, Gurgaon, Haryana and earning more than Rs.9,496/- per month.
Payslips of the claimant for the months of February to April, 2018 have been filed along with the DAR.
27. In the written submissions submitted in the prescribed Form VI-B, the income of the injured is stated to be Rs.9,496/- per month.

28. During cross-examination, the claimant admitted that she has not placed on record any documentary proof to show that she left the job after the accident and suffered any financial loss due to the injuries sustained in the accident.
29. However, the claimant has not been cross-
examined with regard to her testimony that she was earning Rs.9,496/- per month.
There was not even a suggestion put to the claimant that her testimony in this regard is false.
As such, the testimony with regard to her earnings is to be accepted.
30. Keeping in view the nature of injuries and duration of her treatment, this Tribunal feels it just and reasonable to compensate her for loss of earning equivalent to a period of six months.
Therefore, under this head, she is being awarded an amount of Rs.56,976/- (Rs.9,496/- X 6 months).

(iii) Mental and Physical Shock, Pain and Sufferings & Loss of Amenities Sunita Devi vs Shokeen (Shriram Gic) on 23 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3755059/
6 31.
As stated above, the claimant had suffered grievous injuries in the accident.

Though, it is not possible to exactly compensate her for the shock, pain and sufferings etc. which she had actually suffered because of the above injuries, but an effort has to be made to compensate her for the same in a just and reasonable manner.

Hence, keeping in view the extent and nature of the injuries suffered by the claimant and duration of the treatment taken by her etc., an amount of Rs.50,000/-
each is being awarded to her towards (i) mental and physical shock and (ii) for pain and sufferings respectively.
Further, an amount of Rs.25,000/- is also awarded to her towards the loss of amenities suffered by her during said period of her treatment.
Thus, she is awarded total amount of Rs.1,25,000/- under this head.
(iv) Conveyance, Special Diet and Attendant Charges 32.
The claimant in her affidavit deposed that she had spent an amount of Rs.20,000/- on conveyance and more than Rs.300/- per day on special diet for more than six months.
During cross- examination, she admitted that she has not placed on record any documentary proof in order to substantiate her above claims.

Still this Tribunal can very well take note of the requirement of conveyance for claimant for visiting the hospitals and doctors in connection with her treatment and special diet for her early recovery from the injuries suffered because of the accident.
Considering the facts and circumstances of the present case, an amount of Rs.20,000/- is being awarded to the claimant towards conveyance and Rs.30,000/- towards special diet.
33. The claimant in her affidavit deposed that she engaged an attendant to look after her for more than 3-4 months @ Rs.8,000/- per month.

Even though she has not placed on record any document in this regard, keeping in view the nature of injuries suffered by the claimant, she would have required assistance of some family member/attendant for doing her daily routine work for a period of three months.
Therefore, an amount of Rs.8,000/- per month is also being awarded to the claimant towards attendant charges.

The claimant is thus entitled to an amount of Rs.74,000/-
(Rs.20,000/- + Rs.30,000 + Rs. 8,000/- X 3) under this head.

Prasoon Kumar, Senior Legal Executive from their Company as R3W1 who deposed that respondent no. 1 was found to be in possession of fake/forged driving license, permit and fitness at the time of accident and as per DAR, IO has charge-sheeted the driver for the offence committed under Sections 468, 471 and 174 IPC.

38.

Ld. Counsel for respondent no. 3/Insurance Company has argued that since the respondent no. 1 was in possession of forged driving license, permit and fitness, the respondent no. 2 violated the terms and conditions of the Insurance Company by allowing respondent no. 1 to drive.

It is also argued that in view of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy, the Insurance Company can not be made liable to indemnify the respondent no. 2 for payment of compensation to the claimant.

39. In this context, Ld. Counsel for claimant has argued that the respondent no. 2/owner of the vehicle was only required to ensure that the person to whom he is giving the vehicle has a seemingly valid driving license.
It is submitted that the law does not require the owner of the vehicle to get the authenticity of driving license verified from the Licensing Authority.

40. In the present case, there is nothing on record which establishes that the respondent no.
2/owner was aware that the license of respondent no. 1 was forged.
Merely because the permit and fitness of the truck was also forged, the Tribunal can not infer complicity of respondent no. 2 with respondent no. 1 in having forged documents.
41. In the case of United India Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Lehru & Ors., 2003(2) SCR 495, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held the following :-

entities.text: United India Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Lehru & Ors., 2003(2) SCR 495
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence.
If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not.
The owner would then take the test of the driver.
If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.
We find it rather strange that Insurance Companies expect owners to make enquiries with RTO's, which are spread all over the country, whether the driving licence shown to them is valid or not.

Thus where the owner has satisfied himself that Sunita Devi vs Shokeen (Shriram Gic) on 23 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3755059/
8
the driver has a licence and is driving competently there would be no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
The Insurance Company would not then be absolved of liability.

If it ultimately turns out that the licence was fake the Insurance Company would continue to remain liable unless they prove that the owner/insured was aware or had noticed that the licence was fake and still permitted that person to drive.
More importantly even in such a case the Insurance Company would remain liable to the innocent third party, but it may be able to recover from the insured.
This is the law which has been laid down in Skandia 's Sohan Lal Passi 's and Kamla 's case.

We are in full agreement with the views expressed therein and see no reason to take a different view."
42.

The aforesaid issue was subsequently considered by a three-judge Bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of National Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Swaran Singh & Ors., (2004) 3 SCC 297,
wherein it was held that to avoid liability, the insurance company will have to prove that the insured did not take adequate care and caution to verify the genuineness or otherwise of the licence held by the driver.

entities.text: National Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Swaran Singh & Ors., (2004) 3 SCC 297
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paragraphs is as follows :-
"92.

It may be true as has been contended on behalf of the petitioner that a fake or forged licence is as good as no licence but the question herein, as noticed hereinbefore, is whether the insurer must prove that the owner was guilty of the wilful breach of the conditions of the insurance policy or the contract of insurance.
In Lehru case, the matter has been considered in some detail.

We are in general agreement with the approach of the Bench but we intend to point out that the observations made therein must be understood to have been made in the light of the requirements of the law in terms whereof the insurer is to establish wilful breach on the part of the insured and not for the purpose of its disentitlement from raising any defence or for the owners to be absolved from any liability whatsoever."
43.

The aforesaid issue was again re-agitated in the case of Pepsu Road Transport Corporation Vs.
National Insurance Company Ltd., Civil Appeal No. 8276 of 2009, decided by the Hon'ble Supreme Court on 26.08.2013, wherein the following was held :-

entities.text:
Pepsu Road Transport Corporation Vs.
National Insurance Company Ltd., Civil Appeal No. 8276 of 2009
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "8. In a claim for compensation, it is certainly open to the insurer under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) to take a defence that the driver of the vehicle involved in the accident was not duly licensed.
Once such a defence is taken, the onus is on the insurer.
But even after it is proved that the licence possessed by the driver was a fake one, whether there is liability on the insurer is the moot question.
As far as the owner of the vehicle is concerned, when he hires a driver, he has to check whether the driver has a valid driving licence.
Thereafter he has to satisfy himself as to the competence of the driver.
If satisfied in that regard also, it can be said that the owner had taken reasonable care in employing a person who is qualified and competent to drive the vehicle.
The owner cannot be expected to go beyond that, to the extent of verifying the genuineness of the driving licence with the licensing authority before hiring the services of the driver.

However, the situation would be different if at the time of Sunita Devi vs Shokeen (Shriram Gic) on 23 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3755059/
9 insurance of the vehicle or thereafter the insurance company requires the owner of the vehicle to have the licence duly verified from the licensing authority or if the attention of the owner of the vehicle is otherwise invited to the allegation that the licence issued to the driver employed by him is a fake one and yet the owner does not take appropriate action for verification of the matter regarding the genuineness of the licence from the licensing authority.
That is what is explained in Swaran Singh's case (supra).

If despite such information with the owner that the licence possessed by his driver is fake, no action is taken by the insured for appropriate verification, then the insured will be at fault and, in such circumstances, the insurance company is not liable for the compensation."
44. The ratio of law enunciated in aforesaid three cases is that to avoid liability in case of fake driving license, the insurer will have to establish willful breach on the part of the insured.
In other words, the owner has to see driving license of the driver before employing him and if the driving license on the face of it is genuine.
It is not obligatory on the part of owner of the vehicle to get the driving license verified from licensing authority.

The scenario may be different where the owner had knowledge or he came to know through some source that the driver is possessing the fake driving license, as in such cases, the owner is enjoined upon the duty to verify the driving license of driver from transport authority before employing him.
45. No evidence has been brought on record which indicates that the owner of the offending vehicle had reason to believe that the driving license of respondent no. 1 is forged.

In such circumstances, it cannot be said that the respondent no. 2 has committed willful breach of terms and conditions of the insurance policy by giving employment to respondent no. 1 whose license has been proved to be fake by the insurance company.
46. In view of foregoing discussion, it is held that the insurance company cannot avoid its liability and is not even entitled to recovery rights from the respondent no. 2/owner of the vehicle.

Kashmiri Lal 2007 ACJ 688 , this compensation shall be recovered by attaching the bank account of respondent no. 3 with a cost of Rs.5,000/-.

In other words, the owner has to see driving license of the driver before employing him and if the driving license on the face of it is genuine.
